company.name: JAT Holdings PLC
company.sector: Coatings (wood coatings, paints), furnishing and EV chargers

price.note: Traded Rs 35.00–44.00 in April–June 2026 and Rs 32.40–40.20 in July–September 2026; Rs 24.00–55.50 in the year to March 2026.

summary.headline: A growing coatings group, but it earns about 13% on equity against a 20% required return, so the price is far above value
summary.text:
JAT Holdings (JAT.N0000), the wood-coatings maker behind Sayerlack in Sri Lanka, bought Mirotone of New Zealand in November 2025. Sales jumped 36% in the six months to September 2026 and profit to owners rose 24%. At Rs 39.20 the share trades at 1.67x its NAV of Rs 23.48 and 12.6x trailing earnings of Rs 3.10.

The problem is the return. Return on equity has been 11–17% for five years (13% last year, helped by tax losses), while a shareholder should require about 20% here. Growth also needs a lot of cash: stock and customer credit tie up about 64 cents of every rupee of sales, so operating cash flow was −Rs 46mn in the half year and net debt rose to Rs 2.9bn. On the three book-and-earnings methods the fair value is about **Rs 12.00**, about 31% of the price. I'd buy only up to about **Rs 10.20** and treat under **Rs 9.00** as a strong buy. In practice that means not buying at today's price. The fair value was Rs 21.00 in the first analysis (8 November 2026). It is lower now mainly because the required return is now worked out from the beta (20%, against 18% before) and the P/E method uses the P/E those returns justify.

quality.reason: Low debt and a profit every year, but returns are below 15% and profit isn't turning into cash because growth ties up stock and receivables.

tests.label: Return on equity of 15% or more
tests.note: 16%, 15%, 11%, 17%, 13% over 2021/22–2025/26 (average 14.4%); 13.2% over the last 12 months. 2024/25 was lifted by a tax credit and 2025/26 by tax losses.

tests.label: Net debt no more than equity
tests.note: Net debt Rs 2.92bn against equity Rs 12.27bn (Sep 2026), about 1.3x operating profit plus depreciation. Up from Rs 2.19bn in March as stock was built.

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.note: Profit in all ten years of the summary (Rs 0.60–1.78bn). Tax effects swing it: a Rs 0.17bn tax credit in 2024/25 and Rs 0.84bn of tax losses used in 2025/26.

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends
tests.note: Operating cash Rs 0.32bn + Rs 1.31bn over two years against profit of Rs 3.30bn, and −Rs 0.05bn in H1 2026/27 (stock up Rs 1.13bn). Dividends are paid (Rs 0.38bn in Sep 2026) but partly from borrowing.

dividend.note: Rs 0.376bn was paid in September 2026 (the final for 2025/26), about Rs 0.72 a share worked out from the total; the reports don't give the per-share figure.

highlights.title: Sales up 36% with New Zealand
highlights.text: Revenue for the six months to September 2026 was Rs 7.01bn (+36%): Sri Lanka Rs 4.56bn (+14%), Bangladesh Rs 1.56bn (+49%), New Zealand (Mirotone) Rs 0.69bn (new). The September quarter alone was Rs 3.96bn (+37%).

highlights.title: Profit up, but costs rise almost as fast
highlights.text: Gross margin held at 35.1%. Selling costs rose 48% and admin 32%, so operating profit grew 15% to Rs 653mn. Exchange gains cut finance costs 30%. Profit to owners Rs 497mn (+24%), EPS Rs 0.95 (Rs 0.77); Q2 EPS Rs 0.66 (Rs 0.48).

highlights.title: Cash went into stock
highlights.text: Inventory rose to Rs 4.57bn from Rs 3.48bn in March and advances by Rs 0.65bn, so operating cash flow was −Rs 46mn. Total debt rose to Rs 4.38bn and net debt to Rs 2.92bn (Rs 2.19bn in March). Rs 376mn of dividends were paid.

highlights.title: 2025/26: the Mirotone year
highlights.text: Revenue Rs 12.64bn (+9%), gross margin 37.9% (34.5%), operating profit Rs 1.85bn (+1%), profit Rs 1.52bn (−14%; the year before had a tax credit). EPS Rs 2.92, ROE 13%. Mirotone (NZ) was bought on 1 November 2025, with Rs 1.02bn paid for subsidiaries.

highlights.title: Tax will rise
highlights.text: Tax was only 10% of profit in 2025/26 because Rs 0.84bn of tax losses were used; Rs 1.2bn remain. As they run out, tax should move toward 25–30%, taking roughly 15% off profit unless the business grows into it.

models.comment: NAV Rs 23.48 × (ROE − growth) ÷ (required return − growth): ROE 12/14/16% against 21.5/20/18.5%, so about 0.4–0.8x book.

models.name: Residual income

modelsNote: Three methods, averaged; values from scripts/valuation.py. Growth check: assumed 4% / 8% / 12% a year for five years against supported growth of 12.0% (reinvestment rate 89% × return on capital 13.5%, 2025/26, including the Rs 1.02bn Mirotone purchase); all within 2 points. Without the acquisition, reinvestment supported only about 4%, so the base case leans on Mirotone and Bangladesh. Long-run growth 5/6/7% stays below the 12.24% bond yield. The DCF (about Rs 3) is left out of the average because operating cash swings with stock; with it, the fair value would be about Rs 9.75.

scenarios.common: NAV Rs 23.48 and net debt Rs 2.92bn at 30 September 2026; 522.4 million shares. Payout 25%. Residual income starts at 13% ROE. Tax assumed to normalise at about 25% as tax losses run out. Price Rs 39.20 (CSE close, 19 November 2026).

sensitivity.title: Fair value (three methods), Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Bear and bull move with the base. Even at a 14% required return and 18% ROE for good, the methods give about Rs 33, below today's Rs 39.20. The market price assumes either a much lower required return or returns well above anything JAT has earned in the last five years.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 5,270 in total, against Rs 19,600 at Rs 39.20.
buyPlan.realism: Not realistic in normal markets: Rs 10.18 is 74% below the price. This year the share has traded at Rs 32.40–44.00, and its lowest in the last two years was Rs 24.00 (April 2025). Waiting for these prices means, in practice, not owning it unless returns rise well above 15%.

higher: ROE above 16% for two years with tax at a normal rate (Mirotone and Bangladesh earning well)
Operating cash flow close to profit: stock and receivable days falling from about 154 and 139
A lower required return: Sri Lanka's bond yield or default spread falling, or a lower beta on Damodaran's January 2027 figures
Australian sales under the Mirotone brand growing into a meaningful export line
lower: Net debt rising further to fund stock, or another acquisition paid with debt
Margins squeezed as selling and admin costs keep rising faster than sales
Tax rising to 25–30% once the Rs 1.2bn of tax losses are used, without profit growth to offset it
Bangladesh falling back (revenue fell 19% in 2025/26) or Mirotone losing money

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the annual report to March 2026 and the interim reports to June and September 2026. Interim figures are unaudited. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

fullText:
**Summary**

JAT Holdings (JAT.N0000) makes and sells wood coatings (Sayerlack and its own brands), paints, brushes, furniture finishes and Volt EV chargers. It operates mainly in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and since November 2025 in New Zealand through Mirotone. Sales are growing fast: up 36% in the six months to September 2026. But the business earns about 13% on shareholders' money, against the roughly 20% a shareholder should demand here, and its growth ties up a lot of cash in stock and customer credit. At Rs 39.20 the share trades at 1.67x NAV and 12.6x trailing earnings. The methods put fair value at about **Rs 12.00**. I'd buy only up to **Rs 10.20** and treat under **Rs 9.00** as a strong buy. That is far below the price, so it's an avoid at today's price (category 3: it fails two of the four business tests).

**Price and key figures**

- Price: Rs 39.20 (CSE close, 19 November 2026). Range Rs 35.00–44.00 in April–June 2026 and Rs 32.40–40.20 in July–September; Rs 24.00–55.50 in the year to March 2026.
- Six months to September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 7.01bn (+36%), gross margin 35.1%, operating profit Rs 653mn (+15%), profit to owners Rs 497mn (+24%), EPS Rs 0.95 (Rs 0.77). September quarter: revenue Rs 3.96bn (+37%), EPS Rs 0.66 (Rs 0.48).
- By country (H1): Sri Lanka Rs 4.56bn (+14%), Bangladesh Rs 1.56bn (+49%), New Zealand Rs 0.69bn (new), India, Maldives and others Rs 0.20bn. By product: wood coatings Rs 5.08bn (+34%), decoratives Rs 1.08bn (+83%), EV chargers Rs 0.36bn (−5%), furnishing Rs 0.25bn, brushes and rollers Rs 0.23bn.
- Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 12.64bn (+9%), gross margin 37.9%, operating profit Rs 1.85bn (+1%), profit Rs 1.52bn (−14%), EPS Rs 2.92 (Rs 3.50), ROE 13%. Tax was only 10% of profit because Rs 0.84bn of tax losses were used; Rs 1.2bn of losses remain.
- Balance sheet at September 2026: equity Rs 12.27bn (NAV Rs 23.48), inventory Rs 4.57bn (Rs 3.48bn in March), receivables Rs 5.17bn, total debt including leases Rs 4.38bn, cash and short-term deposits Rs 1.46bn, so net debt Rs 2.92bn (0.24x equity).
- Cash: operating cash flow Rs 1.31bn in 2025/26 and Rs 0.32bn in 2024/25 against profit of Rs 1.52bn and Rs 1.78bn; −Rs 46mn in H1 2026/27. About Rs 0.38bn of dividends were paid in September 2026 (about Rs 0.72 a share, worked out from the total).

**Required return**

Beta 1.14: Damodaran's global specialty-chemicals beta (1.04 without debt, January 2026; his emerging-markets file couldn't be opened, so this is provisional) relevered for net debt of 0.14x market value. The only local 5-year beta found was 0.46 (StockAnalysis); the rule takes the higher figure. Cost of equity = 8.24% + 1.14 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = **20.0%** (bear 21.5%, bull 18.5%). That is in the usual 12–22% range for CSE shares. Cost of debt 8.2% (interest paid ÷ average borrowings): about 4 points under the 12.24% bond yield, because most borrowing is short-term import and working-capital loans, some in foreign currency. WACC 18.4%.

**Methods (Rs a share: bear / base / bull → weighted)**

- Justified price to book: 9.96 / 13.42 / 18.38 → 13.37. Book Rs 23.48 × (ROE − growth) ÷ (required return − growth), with long-run ROE 12/14/16% and growth 5/6/7%.
- P/E (justified): 9.19 / 12.24 / 16.63 → 12.21. EPS to March 2027 Rs 2.60 / 3.00 / 3.40 (H1 Rs 0.95 plus a second half of Rs 1.65 / 2.05 / 2.45, against Rs 2.15 last year, with higher tax as losses run out) × 3.5x / 4.1x / 4.9x. The base EPS is 3% below the Rs 3.10 run-rate (12 months to September 2026).
- Residual income: 7.43 / 10.30 / 14.90 → 10.36. ROE fades from 13% to 12/14/16% over ten years, payout 25%.
- **Fair value: Rs 11.98** (average of the three). Buy Rs 10.18 (−15%), strong buy Rs 8.98 (−25%).
- Whole-company DCF (reading only): bear Rs 1.83 / base Rs 2.79 / bull Rs 5.62. Start cash Rs 1.15 / 1.30 / 1.45bn (after-tax operating profit Rs 1.30 / 1.45 / 1.60bn at a normal 25% tax, less non-cash gains; maintenance capex Rs 0.44 / 0.39 / 0.33bn), growth 4 / 8 / 12% for five years, then 5 / 6 / 7%, return on capital 10 / 12 / 14%, WACC 19.7 / 18.4 / 17.1%, less net debt Rs 2.92bn. In the base case 72% of the value comes after year five, and 98% in the bull case. It isn't weighted because operating cash swings with stock levels from year to year, but it makes the main point clear: with a return on capital of about 12% against an 18% WACC, growth adds little value, because each rupee of extra sales needs about 64 cents of working capital. With the DCF included, the fair value would be about Rs 9.75.
- Dividend model: not used, since the payout (about a quarter of profit) is too low for it to say much.

**Growth check**

Supported growth (reinvestment rate × return on capital, 2025/26) is 12.0%: reinvestment of Rs 1.48bn (capex above depreciation Rs 0.10bn, working capital Rs 0.37bn, Mirotone Rs 1.02bn) is 89% of after-tax operating profit, at a 13.5% return on capital. The scenarios assume 4% / 8% / 12% a year for five years, all within 2 points. Without the acquisition, reinvestment supported only about 4%, so the base case relies on Mirotone and Bangladesh. Profit kept × ROE gives 11%. Long-run growth (5–7%) stays below the 12.24% bond yield.

**Capex, maintenance and R&D**

Capex booked Rs 0.42bn in 2025/26 (Rs 0.46bn in 2024/25) against depreciation of Rs 0.33bn, so mostly maintenance; the growth spending went into Mirotone and working capital. The named growth project (a 76% larger acrylic binder plant) has no amount given. The maintenance range is Rs 0.33–0.44bn. R&D is Rs 47mn, 0.4% of revenue, below the 2% needed for an adjustment. Warning: net debt rose by more than half of the year's capex, so expansion has been partly borrowed. Dividends are covered 4x by cash after maintenance capex (2025/26), but in H1 2026/27 they were paid while operating cash was negative.

**Business tests (2 of 4: weak, category 3, unchanged)**

- Return on equity of 15% or more: fail (average 14.4% over five years; 13% last year).
- Net debt no more than equity: pass (0.24x).
- Steady profit: pass (profit every year for ten years, though tax effects swing it).
- Profit turns into cash: fail (operating cash about half of profit over two years, negative in H1).

**Management and plans**

The Chairman, MD and CEO present 2025/26 as the year JAT became a multinational coatings group through Mirotone. Plans: supply Australia under the Mirotone brand from Sri Lankan factories, launch a key new product in Sri Lanka, move into retail and exterior water-based coatings, and grow Volt EV chargers, while keeping expansion "balanced" with financial resilience. Early progress: Australia has started (AUD 0.1mn in H1), New Zealand added Rs 0.69bn of sales, and Bangladesh recovered (+49%). But EV charger sales fell 5%, and the half year's negative cash flow and higher debt cut against the promise of financial resilience.

**Shareholders**

The founder and MD, Aelian Gunawardene, holds 63.63%, and his family about 7% more; Falcon Trading holds 5.18%. Public float is 19.9% (8,741 holders). The top 20 didn't change in the September quarter. Between March and June the Capital Alliance Quantitative Equity Fund cut its stake from 4.62mn to 2.09mn shares.

**Buy plan (500 shares)**

200 at up to Rs 11.98, 150 at up to Rs 10.18 and 150 at up to Rs 8.98: about Rs 5,270 in total (average Rs 10.54), against Rs 19,600 at today's price. This isn't realistic in normal markets: the buy price is 74% below the price, and the lowest in the last two years was Rs 24.00. In practice I'd only reconsider if returns move clearly above 15% with cash flow following profit, or if the required return falls.

**What would change the view**

Higher: ROE above 16% for two years at a normal tax rate; stock and receivable days coming down so cash follows profit; a lower required return (lower bond yields or beta); a growing Australian business. Lower: more debt-funded stock or acquisitions; costs outpacing sales; tax rising as losses run out without profit growth to match; Bangladesh or Mirotone losing money.

**Uncertain or missing**

- The beta is provisional (stand-in sector beta, only one local beta).
- The per-share dividend for 2025/26 isn't stated in these reports; about Rs 0.72 is worked out from the Rs 376mn paid.
- Mirotone's own profit isn't disclosed. The annual report calls it an LKR 489mn investment, while the cash-flow statement shows Rs 1,018mn paid for subsidiaries, which may include other payments.
- EPS and P/E before 2024/25 aren't in the reports read.
